abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents develop software through experimentation, offering an opportunity to design the serving systems supporting their own operation. Effective serving requires coordinating implementation and operating decisions under session dependencies, latency constraints, and correctness requirements. We introduce ServerBench, a benchmark for agentic design of complete, specialized LLM serving systems. Agents experiment against a common objective, dollars per dollar: latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost. Stateful replay preserves session dependencies, and independent verification checks the submitted system. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, $4.87\times$ the vLLM reference; 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems, and 13 exceed the strongest baseline. Our analysis identifies three findings: high-value designs coordinate capacity improvements with load selection; agents interpret performance feedback through workload-relevant experiments; and reliable delivery requires verification of the execution paths introduced by optimization. Overall, ServerBench supports systematic study of how agents translate service objectives and feedback into effective, verified serving systems for given task specifications.

sections.body:
The paper asks whether coding agents can design complete LLM serving systems under deployment and service constraints. It argues that prior benchmarks miss three things: realistic mixed, multi-turn workloads; objectives that include latency targets and GPU cost; and validation beyond output correctness.

ServerBench replays recorded coding-agent sessions, scores each system by latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost, and rebuilds each submission in a fresh deployment for independent checks. Latency targets are the p90 time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT) of an SGLang reference, frozen before development.

The evaluation covers eleven coding-agent models across three deployments. The introduction states that Claude Sonnet 5.5 reaches 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, 4.87 times the vLLM reference.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: ServerBench asks coding agents to build complete LLM serving systems and scores them by latency-qualified value per GPU dollar.

sections.body:
Related work covers two groups. On the inference side, Orca and vLLM address scheduling and memory management, SGLang and Preble exploit prefix reuse, and Sarathi-Serve and DistServe reduce prefill-decode interference. AlphaEvolve and ADRS use evaluator feedback to refine algorithms and system code, and Vortex lets agents refine sparse-attention algorithms in a programmable serving system.

On the benchmark side, KernelBench, ISO-Bench, SWE-Serve, and InferenceBench assess generated kernels, optimization patches, or complete servers. They mostly score correctness and speedup relative to a baseline. The authors state that ServerBench extends this line to response-dependent, stateful sessions and a latency-qualified revenue-to-cost objective.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Existing benchmarks test kernels, patches, or servers under preset conditions, lacking stateful workloads and cost-based objectives.

sections.body:
Each task fixes a checkpoint, GPU allocation, coding-session workload, and service requirements. An agent starts from a minimal Transformers server and has a time budget to produce a submission: an implementation plus a session concurrency.

The score sums the client-measured input and output token value of completed requests whose TTFT and TPOT both meet the targets. It divides that sum by GPU cost over the measurement window, and only verified systems receive a score. Cached input is valued at the full input price, counted once per logical request. The worked example gives USD 3.65 of qualified value over USD 0.83 of GPU cost, scoring 4.40.

Latency targets are the largest p90 values across seeds at a frozen SGLang reference operating point.
sections.heading: ServerBench
sections.headline: Each task fixes the model, GPU allocation, and workload, and scores verified systems by dollars per dollar of qualified token value.

sections.body:
Eleven coding-agent models were run on three deployments. Each agent-deployment pair had one 8-hour development run and a 1,800-second final replay, giving 33 entries. Baselines are SGLang v0.5.19 and vLLM v0.28.0.

Of the 33 runs, 22 yield verified systems and 13 exceed the strongest reference. Claude Opus 5.5 reaches 4.40 on Qwen3.5 9B and 2.64 on Qwen3.8 27B INT4. Results are uneven: six models verify on all three deployments, but only three exceed the strongest reference on all three.

Controlled comparisons and trajectory analysis examine how load and capacity decisions affect value. The authors state that correlations and selected trajectories do not establish causal effects.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: Claude Sonnet 5.5 reaches 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, and 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems.

sections.body:
The conclusion restates the three components of ServerBench: an economic service objective, stateful closed-loop replay, and independent verification. It reports substantial gains across three deployments alongside uneven delivery.

Three priorities follow from the trajectory analysis and controlled comparisons:

- Coordinate capacity improvements with operating load.
- Design experiments around workload characteristics and variation.
- Verify the execution paths that system changes introduce.

The conclusion adds no quantitative claims beyond the evaluation section.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Substantial gains come with uneven delivery, pointing to three priorities for agent-built serving systems.

sections.body:
The stated limitations are:

- Three model-hardware deployments and one coding-trace source.
- Development and final draws share a corpus, and reconstructed inputs do not reproduce original coding tasks.
- Closed-loop replay differs from open-loop production demand, which limits generalization to other architectures, accelerators, and arrival patterns.
- Correlations, source inspection, and selected trajectories do not establish causal effects or design success rates.
- Behavioral tests and code review have finite coverage, and calibration depends on the reference engine.
- Fixed-price token value excludes development and other operating costs, so it is not realized profit.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Results cover three deployments and one trace source, and closed-loop replay with correlational analysis limits generalization and causal claims.

sections.body:
Recorded coding sessions can contain sensitive information, and agent-generated serving code can be unsafe. ServerBench replaces original session content during workload reconstruction and runs generated code in isolated environments with restricted network access. Trace or trajectory releases should be reviewed for sensitive information and checked against source licenses.

Post-run code and action review supports identifying unauthorized behavior. Controlled GPU allocations and resource reporting support responsible use. The authors state that these controls reduce exposure but do not establish that arbitrary generated code is safe.
sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.headline: Recorded sessions are reconstructed without original content, generated code runs in isolated environments, and review does not prove safety.

sections.body:
The appendix contains:

- Task calibration and accounting, including the frozen deployment parameters in Table 2 and API cost estimates in Table 3.
- Replay and reproducibility records, with the reproduction requirements.
- Output verification settings, including the held-out answer test allowing an absolute accuracy decrease of at most 0.1.
- Integrity review and agent configuration.
- Development analysis, controlled design and load comparisons, and observation-window analysis.
- Finding-guided comparisons, including capacity, draft length, replay feedback, and cache repair results.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists deployment calibration, replay records, verification settings, integrity review, controlled comparisons, and finding-guided experiments.
